question.text: Anchoring bias in investing refers to the tendency of an investor to:

answer.text: Follow the investment decisions of other investors in the market
Rely heavily on the first piece of information encountered when making investment decisions
Overestimate their ability to predict market movements
Give more weight to recent events while ignoring historical data

explanation.text: The Logic: Anchoring bias describes the tendency to rely too heavily on the first piece of information encountered (the "anchor") when making subsequent decisions. In investing, the anchor is typically a reference price — the purchase price, an IPO price, a 52-week high, or a recent NAV — and the investor adjusts only insufficiently away from that reference, even when newer information clearly justifies a larger update. The Trap: Following other investors' decisions describes herd mentality / bandwagon bias. Overestimating one's own ability to predict outcomes is overconfidence bias. Over-weighting recent events while ignoring longer history is recency bias. Anchoring is specifically the fixation on an initial reference point, distinct from each of these. Note: The cited workbook (NISM Series V-A — Mutual Fund Distributors, pages 28-30) lists availability heuristic, confirmation bias, familiarity bias, herd mentality, loss aversion, overconfidence, and recency bias, but does not contain an explicit definition or example of anchoring bias. The framing above is standard behavioural-finance knowledge as taught in general investor-behaviour literature.
